title: Plasma-cut a steel plate along a hand-held straightedge until the offcut drops
instruction: Cut the overhanging strip off the plate along the white line with the plasma torch, guiding the torch along the straightedge, then put the torch and the straightedge back where they were and move both hands away.
context: Hand torch cutting is how contaminated steel is cut up where it stands. At Rocky Flats, workers in protective suits cut 240 gloveboxes with plasma torches (DOE); Sellafield's first of 700, in 2024, was cut by hand in air-fed suits. Plasma cutting is routine in decommissioning; robotic glovebox dismantling gave workers under a fifth of the dose of manual cutting, and the sector seeks autonomous cutting (Nucl Eng Des 2026, testing 3 mm glovebox-type plate). DOE carries $539 billion of US cleanup liability (Treasury FY2025). Scrap and ship recycling are hand torch cut too, 'slow, dangerous and tedious', with no general robotic method (IEEE CASE 2021). Cutting torches are involved in about 650 US structure fires a year (25% of non-home hot-work fires, NFPA). About 247,000 US workers do torch-only cutting tasks more than weekly (O*NET, BLS). Makers direct a straightedge guide for straight hand cuts.
setup: Positions in cm from the arm bases' midpoint in x (forward) and the table's centre line in y (+y toward the left arm). A welded steel cutting stand (22 x 14.5 cm, 4 cm tall; x 16 to 38, y -4.5 to 10) is fixed on the table. One 3 mm mild-steel plate, 20 x 21.5 cm (x 17 to 37, y -11.5 to 10), lies on it, held by two blue strap clamps on its left edge at x 20 and x 34. Its right 5.5 cm (0.26 kg) overhangs the stand. A white scribed line 1 mm wide runs the plate's full 20 cm at y -6, from the far edge (x 37) to the near edge (x 17): the cut. Below the line and the overhang, a steel dross tray (26 x 12 cm, 1.2 cm rim; x 14 to 40, y -17 to -5) is fixed on the table. The plasma torch (0.33 kg) lies on two steel rest posts (4.7 cm tall) on a steel base, its yellow glass-filled nylon grip block (30 x 36 x 26 mm) centred at (22, -30): a black handle 26 mm across and 19 cm long along y with a 6 cm stub of lead behind it, and at its +y end a vertical black head 26 mm across and 6 cm tall, pointing down, ending in a copper drag shield 20 mm across whose rim is 2 mm below the nozzle's orifice; the head's axis is 9 cm from the grip block's centre. The straightedge (0.39 kg) lies flat on a black rubber pad (3 mm) at the left: a bright steel flat bar 260 x 25 x 5 mm along x, its working edge the one toward -y, with a steel tab (30 x 88 x 5 mm) welded to the middle of its back edge and a red nylon handle block (30 mm cube) on the tab, centred at (27, 26), 9.5 cm from the working edge. Both grippers start open at the ready pose. The screenshot shows the start. Real trial, fixed settings (full list, tests and safety in the README): a 120 V hand air plasma cutter set to 20 A with shielded drag consumables and dry compressed air as its manual states (bought for about $660 with its compressor, or rented for about $150 a day: products and prices in the README); the torch lead hung from an overhead balancer; the work clamp on the stand, which stands on insulating pads; a witness line scribed on the kept part 20 mm from the cut line with ticks every 5 mm; 10 mm of dry sand in the tray. The robot presses no trigger: the supervisor, outside the screens, holds a hold-to-run switch wired in place of the torch's trigger and closes it only while the shield is on the plate (within 2 mm), between the plate's two edges and within 10 mm of the line; one emergency stop cuts the robots' power and the cutter's output. Welding screens (EN ISO 25980) close the cell, nobody inside; shade 5 filters cover the camera lenses; the cell is outdoors or in an open bay with the cut upwind of everyone and a fan drawing the plume away; welding blankets cover the table and aluminised sleeves the grippers and forearms; a fire extinguisher and a 30 minute fire watch.
scoring: Real trial, read once the parts are under 50 C (how each reading is made: README). The 200 mm line is 40 segments of 5 mm between the ticks. A segment is sound when, over its whole 5 mm: it is cut through (no bridge of metal joins the offcut to the plate; a part snapped or bent off is not cut through); the kept part's cut edge is 18 to 22 mm from the witness line (steel ruler): within 2 mm of the line; the edge is straight (with a steel straightedge laid against it, a 0.5 mm feeler enters nowhere in the segment), which a cut run along the straightedge is and a freehand one is not; an engineer's square on the plate shows no gap over 0.5 mm down the 3 mm cut face (the torch within 10 degrees of square); and no dross bead hangs more than 1.5 mm below the edge and the top corner is not melted back more than 1 mm (overheated: travel too slow, or the torch held still). 0 if the torch or the straightedge falls off the table, or if the video shows the other gripper's fingertips within 45 mm of the nozzle while the arc is on. Otherwise 0.8 x the fraction of the 40 segments that are sound (rounded to 0.001); doing nothing scores 0. 0.9 with all 40 sound and the offcut lying free in the tray. 1.0 with, as well, the torch back on its rest (grip block's centre within 15 mm in plan and 6 mm in height of its start, tilted under 10 degrees, turned under 20), the straightedge back on its pad (handle block's centre within 20 mm in plan and 6 mm in height of its start, flat, turned under 20 degrees), both hands 6 cm or more from the torch, the straightedge and the offcut, and all of them still for the last 1 s. Simulation (stand-ins; full criteria in the README): the arc is on while the torch is in a hand, within 30 degrees of square, its shield's rim from 1 mm into the plate's top to 2 mm above it (nozzle 1-4 mm up), over the plate between its edges and within 10 mm of the line. Each segment gains the arc time spent with the nozzle over it: cut through from 0.241 s (20.75 mm/s or slower, the cutter's maximum for 3 mm at 20 A), overheated beyond 0.787 s (slower than 6.35 mm/s, half the rated 12.7 mm/s). The offcut is a separate body held by one fixed joint per segment; a joint is removed when its segment is cut through, so the offcut drops when all 40 are. A joint also breaks at the load that folds or tears a 5 x 3 mm steel bridge (2.8 N m, 6 kN); a broken joint's segment is not cut through, so an offcut pushed off scores no more than the segments the arc cut. A segment is sound when cut through, not overheated, the nozzle never over 2 mm from the line nor the torch over 10 degrees from square while cutting it, and for 80% or more of its arc time the shield's side within 0.75 mm of the straightedge's working edge with the straightedge flat on the plate.
reset_notes: Simulation: the offcut is put back and its 40 joints restored at reset; lay the torch back on its posts and the straightedge on its pad. Real trial, consumed each time: clamp a new 3 mm plate with 5.5 cm overhanging and scribe the cut line, the witness line and its ticks; empty the offcut and dross from the tray (tongs, once under 50 C) and level the sand; inspect the nozzle and electrode and replace them when the orifice is worn out of round; wipe spatter off the shield and the straightedge's edge.
fidelity: Rigid bodies with real contact: the shield slides on the plate and bears on the loose straightedge, which shifts if it isn't held down. The arc, kerf, heat and dross are not simulated: cutting is arc time per 5 mm segment from the torch's measured pose. The offcut hangs on 40 fixed joints, removed as segments are cut and breaking at a 5 x 3 mm steel bridge's strength (2.8 N m, 6 kN). No sparks, fume, lead drag, warping or kerf loss; cameras unfiltered; no sand in the tray.
